title: Space Complexity in Depth: Stack, Auxiliary and Output
oneLiner: Where the memory actually goes: the call stack, memo tables, copies, the output, and why BFS and DFS use different amounts of it.
keyTakeaway: Space is the PEAK memory in use at any one moment, not the total ever allocated. Count what is live at the worst point: the deepest chain of recursive calls (depth × memory per frame), every collection that grows with the input, and the output if you are counting it. Say separately which part is auxiliary and which part is the answer.
explanation:
Three terms come up in interviews. Total space counts everything, including the input. Auxiliary (extra) space counts only what the algorithm adds, and it is what people usually mean by "space complexity". Output space is the memory for the answer you return. Reversing an array in place is O(1) auxiliary; generating all subsets is O(n) auxiliary for the path and stack but O(n · 2ⁿ) for the output. Saying "O(1) extra, not counting the output" is a complete answer; saying "O(1)" for the subsets is not.

Recursion is the space cost people miss. A function that allocates nothing still uses one stack frame per call that has not returned yet, so its space is the maximum depth of the recursion times the size of a frame. A balanced tree traversal is O(log n); the same code on a tree that has degenerated into a chain is O(n). If each frame also holds its own copy of something (a slice, a path list), multiply: n frames each holding up to n items is O(n²).

Space measures the peak, not the sum. Merge sort allocates a merge buffer at every call, n log n in total over its life, but only one level's worth is alive at a time, so its space is O(n). Naive Fibonacci makes 2ⁿ calls but only ever has n of them on the stack. Garbage that has already been released costs time (the collector has to clean it up), not peak space.

Traversals show the difference clearly. DFS keeps one root to leaf path: its space is the HEIGHT of the tree or the depth of the search. BFS keeps a whole frontier: its space is the WIDTH of the widest level, about n / 2 for a balanced binary tree. So DFS is O(log n) and BFS is O(n) on a balanced tree, while on a long chain it is the other way around. Memoization trades space for time: a memo table has one entry per distinct state, so its size is the state count, and a DP table can often be shrunk to the last row or two when each state only looks back that far.
